analysis.title: The Blue Wave Trade: JPMorgan's "Democrat Factor" Soars 20% As Wall Street Prices A Sweep
key_insights: JPMorgan's Democrat Factor (JP9DEMP Index), a beta-neutral long/short equity pair built to move with Democratic election odds, is up about 20% since August while the S&P 500 rose 2.6% over the same period.

JPM Delta-One calculates that the factor, scaled to a 6% volatility target, has generated ~170% annualized returns since August, versus ~15% annualized for the ~15%-vol S&P. The author notes both figures describe the same ~20% move over roughly ten weeks.

Construction: JPM scores ~3,000 US stocks by sensitivity to changes in Polymarket odds, assigns each an Election Score, and optimizes into two liquid long/short pairs. The Democratic pair is long JP9DEML and short JP9DEMS. The Republican pair (JP9REPP) is long JP9REPL and short JP9REPS.
At the end of September the Dem factor was up 19.45% as Democratic Senate odds rose above 60%, and the Republican factor was down 14.57% as GOP odds collapsed.

JPM attribution shows the move is almost entirely idiosyncratic (stock-specific), with limited explanatory power from traditional risk factors. The factor has been broadly neutral to Beta, Momentum and other factors.

JPM's Manish Sinha (Oct 7) recommended a tactical long in JP9DEMP to add alpha into the election, especially if Polymarket keeps trending toward Democrats. An Oct 8 JPM S&T factor risk note listed 'Long Democrat Pair JP9DEMP' beside hedges for year-end and earnings.

Prediction-market odds of a Democratic sweep rose from 23% of fund managers in BofA's August FMS (47% expected a GOP Senate/Dem House split) to Polymarket at 64% per Hartnett, up from 49% in September. Hartnett shows 28% for a GOP Senate/Dem House split and 9% for a GOP sweep.

Goldman's Alec Phillips finds prediction markets in past midterms (2002, 2006, 2010, 2018, 2022) tended to overstate the challenging party's sweep odds in early October, with an average fade of about 5 points to Election Day. Applied to Goldman's 63%, the sweep odds fall to the high 50s.

Goldman notes midterm polls tend to understate Democrats in Democratic-leaning states and Republicans in Republican-leaning states. The Senate majority runs through Alaska, Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Kansas. CNN's Harry Enten found Republicans hold their best party registration position in a midterm year in at least 20 years in Arizona, Nevada, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.

JPM Delta 1 thematic basket JPMDC26P for a Democratic Congress is long ACA exchange-exposed managed care and hospitals and low-end consumer spending. It is short SMID-cap defense, capital-markets-exposed names, energy permitting beneficiaries and CLARITY Act-dependent names.
The Senate rejected the CLARITY Act crypto market-structure bill 49-50 in mid-September. Every Democrat voted no, along with three Republicans (Collins, Hawley, Moran).

Hartnett: a Democratic sweep 'signals electoral shift from populist capitalism to populist socialism', with tax and regulation direction up, which is negative for EPS. His preferred hedge is short financials and the US dollar.

JPM's Andrew Tyler argues a Blue Wave would fall short of veto-proof two-thirds majorities, producing gridlock that markets typically react to favorably, and says he would be buyers of any dip around the election. The S&P has averaged +5.4%, +11.4%, +12.5% and +14.7% at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months after midterm election days since 1990. All 19 midterms since 1950 showed positive returns at 6, 9 and 12 months.

Goldman's IBD team calls the midterms a potential clearing event: a median 3.5% decline in the month before the vote since 1974 and a median 6.5% gain over the following four months. Pasquariello and Snider cite 12 of the last 13 midterms higher from Election Day through end of February.

Hartnett's scenario map: Democratic sweep is big risk-off (stocks skid more than 10%, dollar and yields fall into year-end, international outperforms). GOP Senate/Dem House split is risk-on (stocks +5%). A GOP sweep is the most bullish surprise. Goldman's Louis Miller warns the result probably won't be risk positive.

The index has not priced the sweep. US stocks are up 13.4% YTD per Hartnett, and the S&P is up only 2.6% since August. The author argues the cheapest election hedge is downside protection on an index that still trades as if the split is the base case, and that the easy money in the factor has been made.

risk_factors: Prediction-market odds could fade about 5 points by Election Day, per Goldman's historical analysis of past midterms.
Midterm polls tend to understate Republicans in Republican-leaning states, consistent with late red-state voters coming home.
Republicans hold their best midterm-year party registration position in at least 20 years in Arizona, Nevada, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.
Gas prices could break either way into the election.
The Democrat Factor trade is crowded and has run about 20%.
A Democratic sweep could mean higher tax and regulation, which Hartnett sees as negative for EPS and a risk-off trigger.
vol_and_positioning: The Democrat Factor trade is described as crowded, both in prediction markets and in the factor space.
JPM S&T's factor risk note recommended buying protection into year-end and earnings given a negative equity risk premium.
The author argues downside protection on the S&P is the cheapest election hedge, since the index trades as if a GOP Senate/Dem House split is the base case.
Goldman's Phillips notes the risk is lopsided: odds cannot exceed 100% while the polling behind the Senate math is shaky.
geopolitical: Trump has ruled out striking Iran before Nov 3, per the article, which ties this to gas prices as a swing factor in the midterms.
US midterm elections on November 3, 2026, with Democrats favored in prediction markets to take both chambers.
cross_bank_references: Goldman's Phillips: prediction markets tend to overstate the challenging party's sweep odds, in contrast to Polymarket's ~64-65% sweep pricing.
Camp one (JPM Tyler, Goldman IBD team, Pasquariello/Snider): midterms are a clearing event and gridlock is favorable.
Camp two (BofA Hartnett, Goldman custom basket head Louis Miller): a sweep is risk-off and the result probably won't be risk positive.
Hartnett's short financials and USD hedge overlaps with JPM's short capital markets leg.

tension_points.bull_case: JPM's Tyler and Goldman's IBD team argue even a Blue Wave yields gridlock, which markets historically favor. S&P averaged +5.4% to +14.7% at 3 to 12 months after midterms, and Goldman cites a median 6.5% gain over four months after the vote.
tension_points.bear_case: Hartnett and Goldman's Miller argue a Democratic sweep is risk-off, with stocks skidding more than 10% on higher tax and regulation, and the market's base case has moved to that scenario.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Prediction-market sweep odds fading about 5 points to the high 50s by Election Day, or a GOP Senate/Dem House split outcome.

tension_points.bull_case: The factor has tracked Polymarket tick for tick, is up ~20% since August, and JPM sees it as a tactical long if odds keep moving toward Democrats.
tension_points.bear_case: The trade is crowded, Goldman's history points to a ~5-point fade in sweep odds, and red-state polls have historically flattered Democrats, so the factor needs odds to go from base case to lock.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A ~5-point slide in Polymarket's Democratic sweep odds, or Polymarket odds no longer trending toward Democrats.
